newsitem.title: UK: U.S. London stocks seek political status quo.
newsitem.headline: U.S. London stocks seek political status quo.

text.p: U.S. stocks traded in London were steady on Tuesday as Americans went to the polls and investors clung to hopes that Republican forces would repel President Bill Clinton's Democrats in the battle for Congress.

London traders said Republican challenger Bob Dole's energetic last-ditch campaign and some opinion polls showing him closing the gap on Clinton had reassured investors who were now seeking solace in the political status quo in the United States.
Clinton's re-election would be acceptable for markets but a landslide victory for his party in Congress would spark a sell-off on fears of a tax and spend policies.
"Clinton gets president and we get no change in Congress. Anything different will be very nasty indeed," one dealer said.
Traders said they expected Wall Street to open 10 or 15 points higher after a solid performance overnight saw it gain 19.75 points. Firm Treasuries would also lend a helping hand.

Dealers said they expected only muted reaction from U.S. equities to Clinton's widely-forecast re-election but any upset in the battle for Congress -- and America's purse strings -- could put pressure on prices.

"Congress is the key because of market fears of runaway spending and uncontrollable deficits under the Democrats...but the chances are the Republicans will hold on there," said Philip Tyson, international economist at HSBC Markets.
Tyson said there were mitigating factors for inflation-wary markets even if the Democrats made substantial inroads.

"The margin of victory in the Senate would have to be particularly large to stop Republicans blocking votes. In the House, the most optimistic scenario sees the Democrats gaining 30 seats which equates to a smaller majority than the Republicans enjoy now," Tyson said.

In addition, he noted that many Democrats openly favoured deficit reduction while Clinton himself had made what he termed fiscally responsible noises and was likely to take steps to reassure jittery markets.

"What this suggests in the worst case scenario if Democrats gain in both Senate and House would be Clinton making some commitment to a balanced budget, suggesting that pressure on Treasuries should be more short term," Tyson said.

Dealers said Dole's 96-hour "March to victory" campaign may have served America and global markets better if it falls just short of propelling the Republican challenger into the White House, given Dole's pledge of extensive tax cuts.
"The last thing we want is for Dole to do a Truman...where he thinks he can fund those tax cuts from is a mystery to me," one trader said.

Dole ended his campaign invoking the spirit of Harry Truman, the Democrat who pulled off one of the U.S.'s greatest political upsets when he defied opinion polls, and an infamous newspaper headline, to defeat Republican Tom Dewey in 1948.
"If Dole made a comeback there would be such uncertainty about the tax pledges and we would see some short-term pressure on markets," HSBC's Tyson said.

Given the market's preoccupation with the elections and Russian President Boris Yeltsin's heart surgery, activity was muted in London on Tuesday. Among U.S. stocks traded in London Texaco dropped $5/8 to $97 on adverse reaction to a federal probe into whether the oil giant tried to destroy documents sought in a racial discrimination lawsuit.
General Motors, which had gained overnight on news it settled a key labour dispute in Indianapolis, was hit by profit-taking on Tuesday, losing $1/8 to $55-1/2.
Among gainers, Apple was up $1/4 at $24-5/8.
